content: The provided text is a detailed and technical document, primarily focused on cervical cancer screening strategies, their effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and associated outcomes. 1. Screening Intervals and Age Groups For women aged 25–50 years, primary HPV screening without triage every 3 years is the most effective strategy, reducing cervical cancer incidence by 70% compared to no screening. For women aged 30–50 years, primary HPV screening every 5 years without triage is highly effective, reducing cervical cancer incidence by 57%. This is closely followed by HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping, which achieves a 56% reduction. Screening every 10 years, starting at ages 35 and 45 (two lifetime screenings), reduces cervical cancer incidence by 33–37%. 2. Effectiveness of Screening Strategies Primary HPV screening without triage is the most effective strategy for reducing cervical cancer incidence across all age groups. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping requires fewer precancer treatment events while maintaining similar effectiveness to primary HPV screening without triage. HPV screening with VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid) or colposcopy triage requires a similar number of precancer treatment events to achieve comparable reductions in cervical cancer incidence. 3. Impact on Women Living with HIV (WLHIV) For WLHIV, primary HPV screening every 3 years for ages 25–50 reduces cervical cancer incidence by 70%. HPV screening with triage options at the same intervals achieves a 64–68% reduction in cervical cancer incidence. 4. Adverse Obstetric Outcomes Primary HPV screening strategies result in fewer adverse obstetric outcomes, such as preterm delivery, compared to VIA-based screening strategies. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage results in 23% fewer adverse obstetric outcomes compared to primary HPV screening without triage. 5. Cost-Effectiveness Analysis Primary HPV screening every 5 years for ages 30–50 is cost-effective in most lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $502 per health-adjusted life year (HALY) saved. Screening every 10 years at ages 35 and 45 is also cost-effective, with an ICER of $154 per HALY saved. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage is nearly as cost-effective as primary HPV screening without triage. 6. Resource Utilization Lifetime costs for cervical cancer screening range from $3 for no screening to $21–$42 for screening every 10 years, $39–$61 for screening every 5 years, and $51–$80 for screening every 3 years. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage results in 31% fewer precancer treatment events compared to primary HPV screening without triage. 7. Follow-Up Management for Positive HPV Tests Women with a positive primary HPV test and a negative triage test should be followed up with repeat HPV testing at 12 or 24 months, depending on the compliance rate. For HPV-colposcopy triage, follow-up testing at both 12 and 24 months is recommended, with referral for colposcopy if any test is positive. 8. Birth Cohort Analysis For women born in 2010 (HIV-positive cohort), it is assumed that 47% will achieve viral suppression with antiretroviral therapy (ART). Sensitivity analysis assumes 100% viral suppression. For women born in 2000 (general population cohort), outcomes represent pre-vaccination screening impacts over the next 20–50 years. 9. Screening Compliance and Sensitivity Analysis Compliance rates significantly impact the effectiveness of follow-up strategies. For example, compliance rates of 90% for follow-up HPV testing at 12 months result in better outcomes compared to lower compliance rates of 70–75%. 10. Key Findings HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage reduces the number needed to treat (NNT) to avert one cervical cancer death by 29% compared to primary HPV screening without triage. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage also results in 36% fewer precancer treatment events and 29% fewer adverse obstetric outcomes compared to primary HPV screening without triage. 11. WHO Recommendations The WHO recommends primary HPV screening every 5 years for ages 30–50 as the most cost-effective strategy for LMICs. For countries with lower GDPs, 10-yearly screening intervals may be considered, particularly for ages 35–45. 12. Conclusion Primary HPV screening, particularly with 16/18 genotyping triage, is highly effective and cost-efficient in reducing cervical cancer incidence and mortality. These strategies also minimize adverse outcomes and resource utilization, making them suitable for implementation in diverse healthcare settings.
